source_user: Contrast MoE with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: A naive dense layer applies one shared feed-forward block to every token; an MoE layer has multiple experts and a router that activates only a selected top-k subset per token. Mechanism: for distributed experts, dispatch scatters token activations to expert owners and combine gathers their weighted outputs, adding all-to-all communication and synchronization that the dense path avoids. Boundary: lower active compute is not proof of lower latency or cost—hot experts, capacity overflow, small batches, memory replication, or limited interconnect bandwidth can dominate. Compare matched quality, precision, hardware, workload, and software, and measure expert load, overflow/drops, communication, memory, latency tails, throughput, failures, and output quality.
risks: Dense and MoE baselines can be confounded by unequal quality, parameter count, placement, or capacity policy.
Routing skew and overflow may cause quality loss or tail-latency regressions hidden by average throughput.
evidence_required: Matched dense comparator, router top-k, capacity and overflow policy, expert placement, topology, precision, workload, and load.
Repeated expert-level load and drop counts, communication traces, memory high-water marks, latency percentiles, throughput, failures, and quality checks.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with MoE. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Two important trade-offs are: (1) routing imbalance—if many tokens select the same expert, its capacity fills while other experts idle, causing token drops, rerouting, queueing, or tail latency; and (2) distributed communication—dispatch and combine can require all-to-all activation traffic, so congested links or synchronization can erase compute savings. Mechanism: the router assigns tokens to top-k experts under a capacity limit, then expert outputs are returned and combined. Boundary: these failures depend on token distribution, batch size, capacity factor, topology, and overflow policy; they cannot be inferred from total or active FLOPs alone. Measure per-expert counts, overflow/drops, communication time, latency percentiles, throughput, memory, errors, and quality against a matched baseline.
risks: Dropped or rerouted tokens can alter model outputs and quality, not merely performance.
Average utilization can conceal hot experts, link contention, queueing, and p99 latency.
evidence_required: Top-k, capacity factor, overflow behavior, load-balancing objective, expert placement, topology, precision, and workload.
Per-token routing and expert histograms, drop/reroute counts, communication traces, latency tails, memory, throughput, failures, and quality evaluation.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with MoE. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Two failure modes are expert hotspots and communication saturation. A hotspot occurs when the router sends too many tokens to one expert; capacity limits can drop or reroute tokens while leaving other expert devices underused. Communication saturation occurs when dispatch/combine all-to-all traffic and synchronization consume more time than the saved expert computation. Mechanism: top-k routing creates token-to-expert assignments, bounded by a capacity policy, followed by scatter, expert execution, and gather. Boundary: severity varies with sequence mix, batch/concurrency, capacity factor, expert placement, and interconnect; a balanced offline batch may not represent serving. Sweep realistic loads and lengths, recording expert load, drops, communication, memory, latency tails, throughput, errors, and quality.
risks: Results may change sharply with routing distribution and serving admission policy.
Performance-only validation can miss output changes caused by overflow, rerouting, or dropped tokens.
evidence_required: Routing and capacity settings, overflow handling, expert mapping, interconnect, workload length/load distribution, and dense or alternative baseline.
Load histograms, overflow/drop/reroute accounting, dispatch/combine timing, memory, latency distributions, throughput, failure logs, and quality checks.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with MoE. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Two trade-offs are (1) capacity overflow: skewed router choices can exceed an expert's token capacity, forcing drops, fallback routing, or extra buffering; and (2) memory and communication overhead: expert weights, activation buffers, routing metadata, and all-to-all transfers can raise peak memory and latency. Mechanism: the router selects top-k experts, dispatches tokens to them, then combines their weighted outputs. Boundary: MoE benefits require balanced assignments and sufficient bandwidth; small batches, long sequences, constrained links, or a low capacity factor can reverse the benefit. Validate with matched workloads and report per-expert load, overflow, communication/compute breakdown, peak memory, latency percentiles, throughput, failures, and quality.
risks: Capacity and fallback choices couple infrastructure metrics to output quality.
Weight and activation memory may be distributed or replicated differently, making naive memory comparisons misleading.
evidence_required: Expert count and placement, top-k, capacity and fallback/drop policy, precision, topology, workload, and matched reference.
Per-expert token accounting, overflow/fallback counts, communication traces, memory high-water marks, latency/throughput, failures, and quality results.

source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Two failure modes are routing imbalance and all-to-all contention. Mechanism: top-k router assignments are exchanged across devices, experts process their assigned tokens, and outputs are synchronized and combined. risks: Mean latency or utilization can hide hot-expert queueing and communication tail effects.
Overflow mitigation may trade performance against altered outputs or quality.
evidence_required: Router policy, top-k, capacity/overflow handling, expert mapping, topology, workload and concurrency ranges, and baseline.
Expert load distributions, drops/reroutes, dispatch/combine and synchronization time, memory, latency tails, throughput, failures, and quality checks.

source_user: Explain how MoE interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: MoE can reduce per-token expert compute because only top-k experts execute, potentially improving throughput or allowing greater total parameter capacity. Mechanism: token dispatch moves activations to selected experts and combine returns their outputs; across devices, all-to-all communication and synchronization add latency and buffering. Memory is not simply active FLOPs: deployed expert weights, replicated/shared layers, activation buffers, routing metadata, and KV cache may determine capacity. Boundary: gains depend on balanced routing, capacity, topology, batch/concurrency, and phase; small batches or skewed serving traffic may worsen latency and throughput. risks: Active parameter count, total deployed memory, and compute cost are distinct quantities.
Average throughput can hide routing-induced queueing, memory pressure, and p99 latency regressions.
evidence_required: Top-k/capacity policy, expert placement and replication, topology, precision, batch/length/concurrency, phase, and baseline.
Phase-specific expert-load and communication traces, overflow, memory high-water marks, latency percentiles, throughput/goodput, failures, and quality checks.

source_user: Explain how MoE interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: For each token, MoE activates only selected experts, which can lower expert computation per token and increase total model capacity. The infrastructure mechanism is a dispatch/compute/combine pipeline: routing sends activations to expert ranks and gathers results, often through all-to-all communication. This can improve throughput when experts are balanced and batches amortize communication, but can increase latency, memory, or both when buffers grow, links saturate, or capacity is exceeded. Boundary: do not generalize from one load point; sequence lengths, concurrency, top-k, capacity factor, topology, and prefill versus decode materially change results. Compare matched systems and measure expert load, communication, memory, latency p50/p95/p99, throughput, drops, errors, and quality.
risks: Communication overlap may make bottlenecks workload- and implementation-dependent.
Capacity overflow and buffering can alter quality and peak memory, especially under skewed traffic.
evidence_required: Router/top-k and capacity policy, expert mapping, topology, precision, workload length and concurrency sweeps, phase, and comparator.
Repeated phase-aware timing, expert token histograms, dispatch/combine traces, memory high-water marks, latency/throughput tails, failures, and quality checks.

source_user: Explain how MoE interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: MoE separates total parameter capacity from active compute: a token may execute only top-k experts, but the service still stores or accesses many expert weights. Mechanism: router assignments cause activation scatter to expert owners, expert computation, and gather/combine synchronization; this adds communication time and temporary buffers. Balanced routing can improve compute efficiency and throughput, while skew, capacity overflow, or interconnect contention can increase queueing and tail latency. Boundary: memory and latency outcomes depend on expert sharding/replication, precision, batch and request-length mix, concurrency, topology, and phase; active-FLOP estimates alone are insufficient. Measure per-expert load, overflow, dispatch/combine time, peak memory, latency distributions, throughput/goodput, failures, and quality against a matched baseline.
risks: Total weights may dominate memory even when active expert compute is small.
Hot experts and communication queues can worsen p99 while leaving aggregate utilization apparently healthy.
evidence_required: Expert sharding/replication, routing and capacity settings, topology, precision, workload/concurrency, phase, and matched baseline.
Expert-load and overflow data, communication/synchronization traces, memory high-water marks, latency tails, throughput, errors, and quality results.

source_user: Explain how MoE interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: An MoE layer may reduce active feed-forward work per token because the router selects only a few experts, which can raise throughput or capacity if routing is balanced. risks: Serving traffic may have routing skew unlike a balanced benchmark, changing memory, throughput, and tail latency.
